title: The One Thing To Settle Before Buying AbbVie Stock - Trefis

AbbVie (ABBV) stock trades at 49.3 times its reported earnings over the past twelve months, compared with 22.9 for the S&P 500. On management’s 2026 forecast for adjusted earnings, which leave out one-time charges, the multiple is about 21. The question is whether its sales keep growing at a double-digit pace. They have so far in 2026, with revenue rising 10.3% in the third quarter from a year earlier. AbbVie has not yet said how fast it expects to grow in 2027, the year a U.S. government-set price starts on one of its larger drugs. That drug is Vraylar, which AbbVie sells in psychiatry and expects to bring in $4.2 billion in 2026. Management has said Vraylar’s price under the IRA drug-pricing rules begins in 2027. AbbVie already sells one drug at an IRA price: Imbruvica. Third-quarter sales of the cancer drug fell 26.1%, which management put down to IRA pricing and competition. A question on what to expect for 2027 came up on AbbVie’s October 30, 2026 call for the third quarter. Because AbbVie had not yet given a formal forecast, an analyst asked about the main pushes and pulls to keep in mind for 2027. Most Of AbbVie’s Growth Comes From Skyrizi And Rinvoq Management has said its two largest drugs, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, are adding $6 billion of sales between them in 2026. That accounts for close to the whole rise in revenue AbbVie expects, to about $67.8 billion in 2026 from $61.2 billion in 2025. Other drugs are growing too, but Humira sales fell 30.6% in the third quarter. The two drugs are expected to bring in $32.1 billion together in 2026, representing close to half of AbbVie’s sales. This means AbbVie’s growth in 2027 depends mostly on how much more Skyrizi and Rinvoq can add, with Vraylar’s new price acting as a drag in the other direction. Management has said it expects top-tier growth again in 2027 and will give its 2027 forecast on its fourth-quarter call, as it typically does. It also said many analysts’ models appear to include Vraylar’s IRA price already. Management expects sales of a newer AbbVie drug for Parkinson’s disease to build gradually, with Medicare coverage more broadly available starting in 2028. These statements offer directions rather than figures. When the company reports its fourth quarter, expected in February 2027, the figure to watch is AbbVie’s 2027 revenue forecast and how much of it management expects from Skyrizi and Rinvoq. title: Why Should AbbVie Stock Holders Watch This One Number? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. AbbVie (ABBV) now draws nearly half of its sales from two drugs. Out of $17.4 billion in total revenue during the third quarter of 2026, the company sold $8.48 billion of Skyrizi and Rinvoq, its two biggest immunology treatments. For a holder, this concentration makes AbbVie stock largely a bet on those two products. So why is AbbVie relying on those two drugs more than it did a year ago? AbbVie relies more heavily on these two drugs because they are growing more than twice as fast as the company as a whole. Skyrizi sales reached nearly $5.8 billion in the third quarter, rising 22.9% on an operational basis that excludes currency moves. Rinvoq sales climbed 24.3% on the same basis, while AbbVie’s total revenue grew 10.5%, also excluding currency. Management gave its reasons during the October 30 call, saying that both drugs continue to beat its expectations and that Skyrizi still wins roughly 1 out of every 2 new or switching psoriasis patients. Humira, another AbbVie immunology drug, is moving the other way. Its sales fell 30.6% to $683 million, a decline management put down to continued biosimilar competition, meaning cheaper copies of the drug. With the two drugs outpacing AbbVie overall while Humira shrinks, Skyrizi and Rinvoq now account for a larger share of AbbVie’s sales than they did a year ago. Other AbbVie drugs illustrate what can cut into a major product’s sales. Humira is not the only treatment losing sales. Imbruvica, a cancer drug, saw its sales fall 26.1% in the third quarter. Management put this drop down to competitive pressure on its market share and to IRA pricing, which was set under a U.S. drug price law. Management also said the IRA price for Vraylar, its psychiatry drug, begins in 2027. Skyrizi and Rinvoq face rivals as well. Management said on the call that the two drugs have been on the market for 8 years and now encounter more competition, including recent oral competition for Skyrizi in psoriasis. Management also said this oral competition is not having a substantive impact on Skyrizi’s share of new patients. Evidence pointing the other way centers on new uses. On October 23, 2026, the FDA approved an under-the-skin starting dose of Skyrizi for Crohn’s disease, an addition management expects will lift Skyrizi’s share of new Crohn’s patients over the next several quarters. Management also expects U.S. approvals of Rinvoq for vitiligo and alopecia areata over the next several months, estimating that these two uses will generate nearly $2 billion of peak sales together. AbbVie has raised its Skyrizi sales guidance for 2026 three times. AbbVie stock trades at 7.7 times sales, compared with 3.3 for the S&P 500. The shares returned 37.5% in the year to November 5, 2026, against 9.9% for the index. The price likely assumes that Skyrizi and Rinvoq will keep growing well ahead of the rest of the company. The stock has not always held up better than the market when trouble arrived. During the 2023 regional banking crisis, AbbVie fell 13.0% while the S&P 500 fell 6.7%. In the 2022 inflation shock, the stock fell only 1.5% while the index fell 24.0%. Each shock picks different winners, which is why building for a crash and a rally beats guessing. A holder should take this reliance seriously, but not as an alarm: for now, Skyrizi and Rinvoq are among AbbVie’s fastest-growing drugs, not its weak spots. For the risk to be worth taking, both drugs need to keep winning new patients as competition grows, enough to make up for Humira’s falling sales. AbbVie is expected to report its fourth quarter in February 2027, and plans to give its 2027 guidance on that call. The share of AbbVie’s sales coming from Skyrizi and Rinvoq, nearly half in the third quarter, is the number to watch in that report. Before you decide on ABBV, consider a better choice. content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. AbbVie (ABBV) stock returned 40.6% in the year to November 4, 2026, against 14.9% for the S&P 500. You may hold it after that run or be thinking of buying. Either way, the company’s profit is hard to project because AbbVie’s net income more than quadrupled in the twelve months to September 2026 from a year earlier. So what would a share bought today be worth if AbbVie keeps growing? Based on AbbVie’s own figures, a scenario shows that a share bought at $294.83 on November 4, 2026, would be worth about $328.03 three years later. That represents an 11.3% upside before dividends. In that scenario, sales grow 9.1% a year, a rate that equals 85% of AbbVie’s latest twelve-month pace of 10.7%. The net margin ends at a blend of 70% of today’s level and 30% of its average at the twelve quarter ends before the latest one. The P/E stays at today’s level. This multiple sits below its 69.5 average at ten quarter ends from December 2023 to September 2026, leaving out readings above 100. The share count stays at today’s level. AbbVie’s diluted count rose about 0.06% over the three years to September 2026, and if that pattern went on, each share would get slightly less. Here is how AbbVie today compares with the scenario three years on. Higher sales produce all of the gain, though the scenario’s lower net margin offsets part of it. None of the upside comes from the P/E. Most of AbbVie’s sales growth comes from its immunology drugs, led by Skyrizi and Rinvoq. Immunology revenue approached $9.2 billion in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, up 16.6% on an operational basis. On its October 30, 2026 call, management said it expects to deliver top-tier growth again in 2027. Management also said Skyrizi and Rinvoq are adding about $6 billion of sales combined in 2026, even with more competition. Skyrizi alone sold $17.6 billion in fiscal 2025, an increase of 49.9% from a year earlier. Those gains have to keep outrunning AbbVie’s losses elsewhere. Humira sales fell 30.6% in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, to $683 million. Management put this decline down to continued competition from biosimilar copies. Management raised its fiscal 2026 revenue outlook to about $67.8 billion. Three of that year’s quarters are already reported, so the outlook is mostly results already in hand, not a pace for later years. How AbbVie’s Upside Changes Under Other Assumptions Each row below changes one assumption while keeping the other two as they are in the scenario. The scenario bases its sales growth on AbbVie’s fastest pace of the past three years. Twelve-month revenue growth was 0.7% in the period to September 2024 and 7.4% a year later. Today’s net margin is also nearly twice its average at the twelve quarter ends from September 2023 to June 2026, so the margin in the scenario is set lower. Taken one at a time, three years of owning AbbVie stock would return nothing, before dividends, if revenue growth slowed to 5.3% a year. That compares with 10.7% in the twelve months to September 2026. Owning the stock would also return nothing if the net margin fell to 12.1% in year three, against 15.7% today. The same holds if the P/E fell to 45.3, against 50.4 at the November 4, 2026 close. AbbVie’s twelve-month net margin is the measure to watch when the company reports its fiscal fourth quarter, expected in February 2027.
